entries.test: NVIDIA's revenue disclosures and customer revenue estimates would show whether revenue outside the Magnificent 7 was continuing to fall sharply.
entries.note: Collapse has a plain reading here as a substantial revenue decline.

entries.test: NVIDIA's FY2026 customer concentration disclosures would establish whether two customers accounted for approximately 36% of revenue.
entries.note: The concentration figure is testable; calling it peculiar and worrying is a value judgment.
The source says 'I think it'll,' rather than assigning a likelihood. Neither the relevant revenue shift nor what counts as an early sign of collapse is specified.
The claim concerns whether the agreements would have been necessary under a counterfactual demand scenario.

entries.test: NVIDIA's investment and guarantee disclosures, together with recipients' purchases, would establish the amounts and revenue relationships.
entries.note: Whether guarantees count as money already spent is part of checking the assertion.

entries.test: NVIDIA's customer concentration, revenue mix and financial sensitivity disclosures would test its claimed complete dependence on continually rising hyperscaler GPU spending.
entries.note: The proposition drops 'maybe' before the customer count and the explicit annual and quarterly spending cadence.

entries.test: A material change in hyperscaler purchasing followed by NVIDIA's financial results and commitment-related losses would test the predicted financial distress.
entries.note: The source covers any change in the purchasing pattern; the proposition narrows that to two examples and changes actual capex cuts to pressure to cut.

entries.test: The original NVIDIA–OpenAI announcements, agreement documents and subsequent disclosures would establish whether a committed $100 billion deal existed and remained active at publication.
entries.note: The plain factual reading concerns the existence and status of a committed deal.

entries.test: Public reporting on negotiations, contingencies, installments and fundraising delays would test whether the round was complicated and difficult to complete.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a concrete meaning for difficult and convoluted.

entries.test: OpenAI's disclosed or publicly reported financial commitments, expense projections and annual losses would test the $655 billion requirement and recurring multibillion-dollar losses.
entries.note: This describes an existing projected funding requirement, not a claim that the spending has already occurred.

entries.test: Public evidence of the stated fundraising difficulty and OpenAI's subsequent business failure would test the conditional survival prediction.
entries.note: The proposition strengthens 'I don't see how it's possible' into an unqualified assertion of failure.

entries.test: OpenAI's eventual shutdown or liquidation would establish the predicted failure to survive.
entries.note: The proposition removes the qualification that the author cannot see a route to survival. There is no deadline.

entries.test: The cited survey's questions and results would establish whether most CEOs reported little or no AI return on investment.
entries.note: Employment and productivity effects are not automatically equivalent to return on investment.

entries.test: Public financing terms, rental contracts and operating costs would show whether full utilization still leaves both companies with losses attributable to debt costs.
entries.note: The source explicitly identifies debt as the cause. Full-utilization economics can be calculated from financial terms.

entries.test: Documented developer trials using contemporary Claude Code would show whether a mid-market SaaS product's core functionality could be reproduced in weeks sufficiently well to prompt consideration of replacing a subscription.
entries.note: The proposition omits the quoted standard of adequacy for a CIO considering a $500,000 renewal.

entries.test: Reproducible trials of contemporary Claude Code would establish whether a single prompt produces a fully formed Salesforce competitor.
entries.note: The source's target is a complete product produced from a prompt.

entries.test: Market event studies, investor reporting and evidence of actual AI substitution for incumbent software would test the asserted sell-off mechanism and its factual premise.
entries.note: The statement combines a rejection of the threat with an explicit claim about what drove share prices.

entries.test: Documented company deployments would show whether firms can straightforwardly replace SaaS subscriptions with software they build using AI.
entries.note: The word 'simply' matters: the claim concerns straightforward replacement, not all in-house development.

entries.test: Published Claude Code success examples, their working artifacts and public training-data evidence would test whether every example fits the asserted toy-and-template description.
entries.note: The proposition loses the explicit universal 'every example' and omits website templates.

entries.test: Publicly documented Claude Code projects and comparisons with existing software would test whether it can produce substantively distinct functionality.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion gives 'unique' a plain reading of substantive differentiation.

entries.test: Documented generation and deployment trials, security and compliance evaluations, and engineering work records would test whether Claude-generated CRM software achieves the listed properties without further engineering.
entries.note: Not automatically deploying is different from being undeployable. The proposition also generalizes from the CRM example and drops 'I assume'.
The source explicitly links lack of knowledge to unreliability. Whether an LLM 'knows anything' has no shared empirical test.
The proposition removes 'do not appear to understand.' The sweeping judgment that no rational basis exists lacks an agreed standard of investment rationality.
The claim expressly includes a private intention to deceive; misleading effects alone cannot establish that intention.

entries.test: The public record available at publication would show whether independent demonstrations, artifacts or verification supported the 30-hour coding and chat-app claims.
entries.note: This concerns the availability of corroborating evidence, not whether the underlying events happened.
Calling deception the primary business model is a polemical characterization without a defined factual threshold.

entries.test: Anthropic's cited marketing statements, omitted qualifications and publicly documented product results would show whether the statements materially misrepresented the demonstrated capabilities.
entries.note: The following examples supply specific alleged omissions and misleading representations, giving the accusation factual content.

entries.test: A review of contemporaneous praise articles, their authors' software experience and the demonstrated outputs would test the assertions about who supplied the praise and what the examples showed.
entries.note: The source's 'mostly' qualifies the authors of praise articles, not the proportion of Claude Code's output that regurgitates training data.

entries.test: The 2025 METR study's reported completion-time effects and participants' perceived speed changes would settle the two percentages.
entries.note: He states this in his own voice while attributing the evidence to METR; the proposition retains that study scope.
Both 'grifter economy' and 'asleep at the wheel' function as broad condemnatory metaphors.
